objectives:
This course introduces the mathematical foundations of modern cryptography. We begin with classical and public-key cryptography, including modular arithmetic, Diffie–Hellman, RSA, discrete logarithms, elliptic curves, and digital signatures. We then introduce the modern notion of security through adversarial games, advantage bounds, negligible functions, and reduction proofs. The final part of the course studies cryptography in the quantum era, including Shor’s algorithm as a threat model, lattice-based cryptography, NTRU, Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA, and hash-based signatures.
Prerequisties
Students should know linear algebra and basic proof-writing. Prior abstract algebra, number theory, or probability is helpful but not required. Basic programming experience is recommended for optional computational assignments.
content:
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

Explain the mathematical structure behind RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ElGamal, elliptic-curve cryptography, and digital signatures.
Analyze the hardness assumptions behind factorization, discrete logarithms, elliptic-curve discrete logarithms, and lattice problems.
State formal security notions using adversarial games and advantage functions.
Write simple reduction proofs showing that breaking a cryptographic system would imply solving an assumed hard problem.
Explain why quantum computers threaten RSA, DSA, ECDSA, and ordinary Diffie–Hellman.
Describe the basic mathematics behind lattice-based and hash-based post-quantum schemes.
Compare classical public-key systems with current post-quantum standards such as ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA.
books:
Main texts and references

Required main text:
Jeffrey Hoffstein, Jill Pipher, Joseph H. Silverman, An Introduction to Mathematical Cryptography, 2nd ed., Springer, 2014.

Supplementary texts:
Mike Rosulek, The Joy of Cryptography, for game-based security, adversarial advantage, pseudorandomness, CPA/CCA security, signatures, and post-quantum overview.
Jonathan Katz and Yehuda Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography, 3rd ed., for rigorous modern definitions and proofs.
Dan Boneh and Victor Shoup, A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography, for advanced proof frameworks and examples.
NIST PQC standards: FIPS 203 ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA.
